The video editing process is labor-intensive and requires a deep understanding of its creative aspects. To streamline this process, AI-assisted video editing has emerged as a potential solution. However, the development of these AI tools heavily relies on the availability of large video editing datasets. Unfortunately, current datasets are limited in their scale, diversity, and complexity, hindering their effectiveness. To address this limitation, we introduce a comprehensive video editing dataset called StruEdit, which contains 1,000 high-quality videos edited by human experts. Unlike existing datasets, StruEdit includes diverse content, such as 1,000+ unique shots, 500+ transitions, and 200+ effects, as well as 100+ editing actions across 15 different categories. We also provide a set of benchmarks to evaluate the performance of AI models in processing video editing signals and their components. Experimental results indicate that StruEdit significantly outperforms existing datasets in these evaluations. The code and data for StruEdit are available on the GitHub repository "github.com/SHI-Labs/StruEdit". For more information, please visit the project website at suanmingchen.github.io/StruEdit. In the context of offline reinforcement learning, the goal is to develop a policy that achieves the highest possible return value given a fixed dataset as a reference. This paper explores the scenario where the policy only undergoes a limited number of observations before being evaluated. This limited examination approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios where updating the policy after evaluating each action would be impractical due to high costs or time constraints. We propose a framework for analyzing the rate of convergence for policy optimization under this limited examination condition, and show that our framework can be applied to various offline reinforcement learning problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework can be utilized to design a first-order optimization-based policy optimization method that converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\frac{M}{n}})$ under the condition of $M$ initial explorations and $n$ collected data samples. Notably, this rate is comparable to the rate achieved by the state-of-the-art first-order method under the condition of unlimited explorations. Additionally, we propose a practical policy optimization method that converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$ under the condition of $M = 1$ initial exploration and $n$ collected data samples. We validate the efficacy of our proposed methods through a series of experiments. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/Chenyu-Han/Policy_Optimization_Limited_Examination. A key objective of many electronic design automation tools is to create an optimized design with the most efficient implementation possible. Neural machine translation significantly enhances language translation capabilities, especially for resource-constrained languages. However, NMT systems trained on limited data often produce translations that are far removed from the original target. To address this issue, researchers have explored using cross-modal alignment techniques that utilize both source and target sentences in a joint attentional mechanism. Although these methods have shown promise in improving translation quality, they require substantial training data. This study investigates the effectiveness of cross-modal attention for low-resource languages using two datasets and evaluates its performance against monolingual augmentation and backtranslation. The results demonstrate that cross-modal attention can reduce translation errors by up to 20% and achieve comparable performance with the augmented methods. Notably, it outperforms these methods in terms of fluency and is particularly beneficial for languages with limited training data available. The study also highlights the potential of cross-modal attention as a standalone method for low-resource languages. We focus on a second-order torsion problem, considering a bounded domain Omega with a smooth boundary. At Omega's boundary, we impose Robin boundary conditions represented by the coefficient alpha. Our analysis demonstrates that, for any given alpha, the solution to the torsion problem exhibits infinite stiffness when the domain Omega becomes increasingly small. Notably, this phenomenon is distinct from the behavior observed in the case of pure Neumann boundary conditions, where the solution remains finite for any alpha greater than -1/2. Furthermore, we derive a specific stiffness estimate for the Robin problem, valid in the limit of Omega approaching zero. This result stands in contrast to the findings of a previous study [8], which reported a stiffness estimate for the Neumann case, but with a logarithmic correction not captured in our work. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that this correction is nonessential, estimating the solution's growth within a constant factor relative to the standard O(1) behavior. Our proof relies on a combination of mathematical operators, including the single layer operator, the double layer operator, and the fractional Laplacian, as well as a small perturbation approach. This approach allows us to establish a specific small angle condition, under which the solution exhibits stiffness. Our method is distinct from the strategy employed in [8], which relied on a representation formula for the double layer operator and the concept of a logarithmic derivative. Additionally, we discuss the potential implications of this stiffness phenomenon for the study of asymptotic behavior in related problems, including the Robin eigenvalue and the associated asymptotic behavior of the torsion problem. The issue of bird species identification is a complex one, driven by the growing need for effective bird conservation. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel multistage learning-based approach that utilizes a pre-trained VGG16 model. This approach involves a two-stage training process, initially using the entire dataset to fine-tune the model's fully connected layers, and subsequently using the entire dataset to fine-tune the layers that distinguish specific bird species. Through this process, we have achieved a classification accuracy of 91% in identifying bird species. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the feasibility of transferring our model to a new, smaller dataset with a significantly reduced number of images, achieving an impressive 84% classification accuracy. We demonstrate CacheQL's capabilities by implementing a software-fingerprinting attack that accurately identifies 20 widely used production libraries with up to 99.1% accuracy, including several popular open-source projects such as Apache Arrow, Apache Spark, and Hadoop, as well as popular JavaScript libraries like Lodash. Given $n$ line segments of length $1$ and an integer $k$, the task is to connect these segments into a simple polygon within a $n$-times-2 grid by selecting $n$ vertices at most. The goal is to choose these vertices such that the resulting polygon is both simple and contained within the grid. We demonstrate that the decision version of this problem is NP-hard, showing that solving it requires a significant number of computational steps unless a fundamental problem in computational complexity has a breakthrough solution. Furthermore, we establish that the problem also has inherent computational difficulties. Additionally, we prove that the problem of determining the minimum number of vertices required to connect these segments into a simple polygon is computationally intractable, even in the case where the segments are all parallel to each other. This establishes a fundamental limitation in computational complexity theory. Finally, we examine a special instance of the problem where the segments are all parallel to each other and show that, in this case, the problem can be solved efficiently when there are exactly $n-1$ segments, but remains computationally difficult when there are more than $n-1$ segments. These results are based on the concept of "separators" and a related problem in computational geometry. The key to these proofs is a new algorithm that connects these segments into a simple polygon using the fewest possible vertices, as well as a new geometric property of simple polygons. The mathematical concept of "hamiltonian cycles" is also used to establish the computational difficulty of the problem. A novel blind multi-picture steganography technique, called SABMIS, has been proposed for image data. This method leverages the sparse signal recovery approach to create a hidden message from a cover image. The cover image is divided into two parts: a clear signal and a steganographic message. The clear signal is preserved, whereas the steganographic message is embedded into a cover image. The hidden message, comprising the clear signal and steganographic information, is then recovered from a distorted image. The quality of the recovered image is measured using a metric based on the 20:1 cover-to-hidden signal ratio, demonstrating an error rate of less than 3%. This method outperforms existing methods, achieving a 3% decrease in error rate. The experimental results also show that the recovered image exhibits better visual quality than the original cover image. The technique's performance is further evaluated in terms of its robustness against various image processing operations, such as compression, denoising, and watermarks. The findings confirm the superiority of SABMIS over existing steganography methods. The proposed approach is also compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods, revealing its advantages in terms of performance and robustness. The ability of deep neural networks to learn complex image representations has significantly enhanced image classification performance. The edge computing model has been further enhanced by the integration of mobile devices such as vehicles, leading to the creation of a unique edge federated training network. The experimental results demonstrate that FedAV achieves superior outcomes compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, with a notable 12.5% improvement in accuracy and a 28.6% reduction in communication costs. Location-based services have become increasingly popular, with the internet providing essential information such as nearby restaurants, public transportation schedules, and service provider locations. However, users' privacy concerns often hinder the effectiveness of location-based services, as service providers may struggle to locate users accurately. To address this issue, a novel approach utilizing edge computing has been proposed to provide location-based services while maintaining users' anonymity. The method involves users calculating their distance from nearby access points and sharing the measurements with service providers, who can then estimate the user's location using these values along with access points' locations. To optimize this process, a machine learning-based algorithm has been developed, leveraging a random forest approach to provide location estimates. The results show that this method significantly outperforms the traditional distance-based location calculation, with a mean error reduction of 44.6% and 50.6% on two real-world datasets. Furthermore, the proposed approach has been demonstrated to provide robust location estimates, with a mean error of 0.08 km and 0.09 km on the two datasets. The results also highlight the benefits of using edge computing, with the edge computing-based method achieving a 30% performance gain compared to the cloud-based method. To validate the privacy aspects of this approach, a comprehensive security analysis was conducted, confirming that the proposed method respects users' anonymity. The results of this study will guide future research in location-based services and edge computing, with the aim of providing location-based services while maintaining users' anonymity. The False Discovery Rate (FDR) control is a preferred alternative to the traditional Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) control in multiple testing scenarios. However, the existing FDR control methods are limited to independent observations. In this research, we introduce a new method to control FDR for dependent data, achieving the same level of significance as the false coverage rate (FCR). Our approach is based on the generalized linear combination (GLC) estimator of local false coverage rate (LCER), which we modify to account for dependence. We derive the asymptotic behavior of the GLC estimator of the log false discovery rate (logFDR) and demonstrate its consistency. Furthermore, we establish the asymptotic normality of the GLC estimator and the GLC-based test, which enables FDR control. Our approach is applied to the dependent t-test and the independent symmetric test, and the results show that the GLC-based test outperforms the independent symmetric test in terms of power. Additionally, the GLC-based test exhibits improved power compared to the LRT-FDR and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedures, while maintaining the same level of FDR control. Our approach is illustrated using real-world data from the COVID-19 pandemic and the human microbiome. The performance of our method is compared to the existing methods using simulation studies, which show that our approach is more powerful than the existing methods, while maintaining the same level of FDR control. Our R package, glfdr, provides the GLC-based test for dependent data, offering a new approach for FDR control in multiple testing scenarios. This package is available on CRAN and the source code is hosted on GitHub. The proposed method can be applied to the dependent t-test and the GLC-based test, which are available for download. A melanoma skin cancer diagnosis requires prompt action, as it spreads rapidly and is preventable with early detection. To raise awareness about melanoma and its treatment, we developed a distributed education and detection system. This system consists of a personalized health tool and a categorization method for melanoma and non-melanoma images. The former is a mobile application that guides users in identifying potential melanoma, while the latter is a machine learning model trained to classify images of skin lesions as melanoma or non-melanoma. Voice conversion, a technique to transform the voice of a source speaker into that of a target speaker while retaining the original voice's identity and speech capabilities, has been an area of active research. Traditional methods for voice conversion have been based on statistical models that rely on pre-defined acoustic units, but these approaches often fail to capture the complex relationships within speech data. In this study, a new voice conversion method called DiffSVC has been developed, drawing from the success of recent speech generative models. DiffSVC utilizes a diffusion probabilistic model to generate speech by gradually adding noise to speech data, which it learns from a target speaker's voice. This approach enables the creation of high-quality speech that is both natural-sounding and easy to understand. Experimental results show that DiffSVC outperforms traditional voice conversion methods in terms of both speech quality and identity preservation. Additionally, DiffSVC has been found to be more effective in voice conversion tasks involving unseen speakers and unseen speech styles. Its code has been made publicly available for others to build upon. As far as the researchers know, this is the first diffusion probabilistic model to be applied to voice conversion tasks. This work is expected to open up new avenues for voice conversion research and inspire the development of new voice conversion methods. As such, it has the potential to significantly impact the field of voice conversion and speech research. To overcome this limitation, we propose an unsupervised domain adaptation method that utilizes feature disentanglement and graph convolutional networks. Our approach involves training a domain-invariant GCN to extract class-relevant features from medical images, while employing a variational autoencoder to disentangle semantic and domain-specific features. Experimental results on two medical image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving high classification accuracy under domain shift conditions. Additionally, our results are extended to encompass a broader class of functions $g(x)$ and $f_\alpha(x)$. The implications of our findings are then applied in the investigation of the convergence properties of the gradient descent algorithm for minimizing convex sums of measurements, particularly in the context of the $\ell_p$ family, where $p \geq 1$. Our analysis reveals that the convergence rate of the gradient descent algorithm for this family of convex functions is $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k^{\frac{2}{(p+1)}}})$. This finding is then extended to encompass the convex sum of measurement functions defined on the Grassmann manifold. Finally, our results are applied in the development of a novel algorithm for the recovery of sparse signals from noisy measurements obtained from the Grassmann manifold. This paper introduces the concept of greater rank numerical domains and unitary expansions as a means to further develop the unitary cone algebra. Building upon the existing greater rank domains by Moore and Sheridan, this work extends their theory to numerical domains and investigates properties such as multiplicative order. Key findings reveal that the multiplicative order of a domain $D$ in a cone algebra is equal to the multiplicative order of $D^+$ and rank $D$ minus rank $1$. Additionally, this work demonstrates that the cone algebra operations are continuous with respect to a specified topology, and we define and characterize unitary expansions within this context. Furthermore, this theory is applied to algebraic unitary expansions of semidefinite programs. Finally, this work presents several illustrative examples to demonstrate the utility and applications of greater rank numerical domains and unitary expansions. We calculate the leading order transverse mass distributions in W boson creation processes, including W+jet and W+gamma production, up to third order in QCD corrections, representing the highest level achieved to date. Our analysis reveals that the third order QCD corrections yield substantial outcomes, significantly impacting both W boson plus jet and W boson plus gamma calculations. For the W+jet scenario, these corrections result in a 1.4% change in integrated transverse momentum and a 60% shift in its mean value, largely due to real correction emissions. In contrast, the W+gamma process exhibits a 0.6% change in integrated transverse momentum at its next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order order. Our findings are crucial for refining W boson mass measurements at the LHC. Moreover, the results provide essential insights into the role of QCD dynamics in the transverse momentum distribution of particles produced in high-energy collisions. Our analysis also includes a detailed examination of the charge imbalance parameter, representing a new observable with the potential to distinguish between different W boson production channels. In particular, the results for the W boson plus jet channel show a 0.3% change in its mean value at its next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order order. Our calculations also include a comparison with the conventional MadGrap+OpenLoops method, highlighting discrepancies between this approach and our results. Point cloud resampling, an essential step in point cloud processing, aims to reduce the density of a point cloud by selecting a subset of points while preserving the overall shape. Despite its importance, this task is challenging due to the lack of information about the selected points and the need to avoid distorted shapes in the resampled point cloud. This paper presents a new approach to point cloud resampling, leveraging a hypergraph-based method that effectively captures point relationships in the original cloud. By analyzing these relationships, the approach can identify the most informative points to include in the resampled cloud, ensuring a high-quality outcome. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in producing resampled point clouds that are not only well-shaped and smooth but also capable of withstanding compression, thus enhancing their robustness. Additionally, the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of resampled point quality and shape preservation, making it a promising solution for point cloud processing applications. This study explores the application of carbon dots extracted from cigarette smoke for bio-imaging purposes. By analyzing the dots' fluorescent properties, we discovered that they emit light at two specific wavelengths when exposed to excitation light of 405 and 488 nm wavelengths. Our results indicate that these carbon dots exhibit a unique type of fluorescence known as delayed fluorescence, which occurs after the initial light excitation. We also found that the intensity and duration of this delayed fluorescence are directly related to the concentration of the dots. By using a bio-imaging technique, we were able to observe the distribution of the dots within living cells and found that they accumulate primarily in the cells' vesicles and membranes. Our findings suggest that these carbon dots may have potential applications in bio-imaging investigations. This research paves the way for further studies on the bio-imaging capabilities of carbon dots derived from cigarette smoke. A dead pixel is a faulty point within an image sensor that consistently produces a zero value, often used to identify such issues in images captured by faulty sensors. However, the conventional method of detecting dead pixels relies on capturing images with the camera lens at multiple positions, leading to a significant increase in capture time. This issue is addressed by introducing a novel dead pixel detection approach, which employs a computational model to derive a low-rank matrix representing the image formation process. This model-based method is able to identify dead pixels without the need for actual camera capture, and its computational efficiency is further enhanced by utilizing an efficient receptive field. Our proposed method was evaluated on both artificial and real-world image datasets, and the results demonstrated its superior performance in terms of both accuracy and speed compared to the traditional image-based approach. Additionally, the proposed method was found to be more effective in detecting dead pixels in real-world images, and its computational efficiency makes it a suitable solution for real-time dead pixel examination. This method is also applicable to a range of other image reconstruction tasks, such as inpainting and denoising. Our code for the proposed method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/SeokbeonPark/EfficientReceptiveField. We introduce AppealNet, a highly-efficient collaborative architecture for deep learning inference that effectively balances the performance requirements of advanced deep learning models with the limitations of mobile devices. By integrating a novel decision-making algorithm that determines which tasks can be handled by a mobile device with a sophisticated reconfigurable hardware design, AppealNet optimizes both processing speed and power consumption, while providing a flexible design that can be easily implemented using off-the-shelf components. In contrast to existing approaches, AppealNet achieves superior performance, with significant reductions in inference latency and energy consumption, ranging from 6.8x to 10.3x, with comparable or better accuracy. Additionally, AppealNet demonstrates substantial energy savings, with an average reduction of 6.8x, 7.3x, or 8.3x, while maintaining high system utilization efficiency, ranging from 76.5% to 90.1%. Our results also show that AppealNet's design can be easily extended to support more complex deep learning models, such as YOLOv4, with substantial improvements in both accuracy and efficiency, including a 6x reduction in energy consumption, 6.3x reduction in inference latency, and 77.6% higher system utilization efficiency, compared to the state-of-the-art approach. Finally, AppealNet's design can be easily scaled up to support large-scale systems, with significant reductions in energy consumption, ranging from 5.6x to 9.3x, and high system utilization efficiency, ranging from 76.4% to 89.1%. Overall, AppealNet represents a highly-effective and efficient solution for advanced deep learning applications. The code for AppealNet is available on GitHub.

In the realm of multi-armed bandits, we've introduced a novel framework called "assist optimality," which assesses the effectiveness of assistive signals in reaching the optimal policy with a specified level of confidence. This approach is particularly useful in scenarios where individual decision-making is unreliable. Our framework is applicable to both adaptive systems and environments. To demonstrate its utility, we've developed a "cuckoo screen" that dynamically adjusts its size based on performance, serving as an adaptive measure of the difference between the decision-making system's value and the optimal value. This enables us to create an "assistive UCB" algorithm that ensures sublinear regret while identifying the optimal signal with a specified level of confidence, even in the presence of unreliable decision-making. Our findings are further validated by simulations of a driving assistance system. This research has significant implications for addressing challenges in complex, multi-agent settings where decision-making is imperfect. A common misconception in deep learning is that neural network functions must have a real co-domain. A closer examination, however, reveals that this assumption is unwarranted; complex-valued outcomes are theoretically possible. While the field of complex-valued neural networks acknowledges this possibility, it lacks concrete evidence. This paper provides empirical backing by demonstrating that certain complex-valued functions, such as those defined on the complex unit circle and plane, can be represented by complex-valued deep neural networks. Furthermore, we show that these complex networks are capable of approximating any given continuous function, as opposed to their real-valued counterparts which can only handle continuous and differentiable functions. This breakthrough has significant implications for the field of complex-valued neural networks and offers a foundation for future explorations of this area. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the complex derivative and its relevance to complex-valued functions, highlighting its potential applications in the field. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive and nuanced perspective on the role of author metrics in academic evaluation. We also aim to encourage authors and their institutions to consider these metrics as part of their overall reputation, offering a unique view of an author's contribution that complements other evaluation methods. The rapid growth in IoT device deployment has led to a surge in offloading capabilities, shifting computation from resource-constrained devices to cloud data centers. In contrast, a novel approach called Self-Managed IoT has been proposed, enabling users to offload tasks to nearby cloudlets with or without cloud involvement. This system allows users to select the most suitable cloud or data center based on their needs, offering a high degree of control. Experimental results using IoT offloading applications demonstrate Self-Managed IoT's effectiveness in providing efficient offloading solutions. Additionally, user studies have shown that users value full control and the potential for IoT devices to offload tasks more frequently than previously thought. Self-Managed IoT's potential has also been demonstrated through successful implementation on IoT development boards. This study introduces a novel approach where a tethered aerial robot employs physical contact to guide a human's hand to desired locations on a given surface. Our method utilizes the tether as a constraint to circumvent the need for explicit human pose estimation or external tools. A customized regulator for the aerial robot is developed, incorporating human state awareness to account for dynamic changes in the human's hand pose. This includes a novel error term that leverages measurements from the tether to estimate the human's pose, and experiments demonstrate improved performance compared to a basic regulator. Our approach is validated through experiments conducted in various settings. One experiment showcases the ability of the robot to direct a human's hand to specific points using only tether feedback, and another demonstrates the benefits of incorporating human state awareness for navigating around obstacles while still guiding the human's hand to target locations. Additionally, a simulation study confirms the efficacy of the proposed method in scenarios where tether length measurements are subject to noise. Both experiments and simulations are conducted using a 3DOF robot with actuated joints. Our method's source code is publicly available on the GitHub platform. You can access it at: https://github.com/UTIA- Robotics/human-state-aware-regulator. This research is a significant contribution to the field of human-robot interaction through physical contact, and the authors believe that it has the potential to be applied in various human-robot collaboration tasks, such as guiding objects and assisting with manipulation. Furthermore, the proposed method can be extended to scenarios where the human's pose is to be estimated for other purposes, such as tracking or following. This research also opens up possibilities for future research directions, and the authors look forward to exploring these possibilities. However, even with these uncertainties, it is possible to make predictions about the universe's early stages that can be tested with future observations. This study investigates the application of deep convolutional neural networks to identify spoken utterances as positive or negative speech in videos, leveraging the YouTube Speech dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of using frame-level sentiment predictions to identify spoken utterances in a sentence, even when the utterances are interrupted by background conversations. We also examine the benefits of using pre-trained neural networks pre-trained on ImageNet for sentiment classification tasks. Our baseline results show that a pre-trained neural network achieves a 53.3% accuracy in classifying utterances as positive or negative. We further enhance the network's performance by incorporating a multi-modal approach that combines utterance and frame-level predictions, yielding a 64.2% accuracy on the test set. Our research also reveals that the pre-trained neural network exhibits robust performance across various evaluation metrics, including AUC, F1, and EER. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the pre-trained neural network outperforms a traditional approach that uses a support vector machine to classify utterances, even when the utterances are short and lack contextual information. Our results also indicate that the pre-trained neural network exhibits a strong ability to generalize to new, unseen speakers and videos. Finally, we explore the potential applications of our approach in real-world contexts, such as sentiment analysis, human-computer interaction, and speech-to-text analysis. Our research contributes to the ongoing efforts to develop more effective, transferable, and robust deep learning models for various natural language processing tasks. It examines the performance of these models using a test dataset of death occurrences in a specific country, focusing on predicting mortality for the upcoming year. The resulting directional asymptotic cones are abstract versions of directional bi-proximal groups, a concept initially introduced by E. Moiseev and A. Dranishnikov, but under a different framework. We demonstrate that these directional asymptotic cones are either isometrically embeddable into Euclidean space, a linear group, or split Lie group, or form a linear group, a solvable group, or a central dimension 1 group, depending on specific conditions. The paper also includes an application of this theory to the study of solvable groups, which are defined by their metric properties. Monod. The full text of this paper is available at arXiv:1108.3060. Additionally, we provide a solution to another problem related to the asymptotic cones of groups, originally proposed by G. Levitt, which describes the solvable groups that can be represented as asymptotic cones of connected groups. We investigate the computational capabilities of context-free grammars with selection languages that ensure unique choices are made. Our research focuses on locally testable languages, which can be recognized by finite automata, and find that the resulting class of languages constitutes a closed operator on strings, but does not capture all context-free languages. Furthermore, we show that the closed operator on locally testable languages yields the same powers as context-free grammars with choice between a finite number of languages, and that both classes are capable of capturing regular languages. Additionally, we show that the minimal context-free languages in these classes have linear size with respect to input length. Our research also demonstrates that the problem of decidability for a language being context-free is solvable within these classes. The findings of our research have implications for the fields of natural language processing and programming language semantics. Deep learning models often produce biased outcomes, which can be particularly problematic in high-stakes situations such as loan approvals and job placements. This bias can be found in the loan data from the Federal Reserve Board, where individuals from certain racial or ethnic groups may have a disadvantage. To address this issue, we propose a novel adversarial acquired fairness approach that modifies the loss function to ensure fairness. Our method incorporates two key components: dampening to reduce existing bias and piling to introduce new bias. By adjusting the dampening and piling coefficients, we can achieve a balance between maintaining existing fairness and introducing new bias. Our experiments demonstrate that our method is effective in reducing bias in both tabular and image-based datasets. Furthermore, we found that our method is more effective than existing state-of-the-art fairness algorithms. Our code is available on GitHub. This paper investigates the load of a single server queueing system under specific conditions: arrivals are randomly distributed, service times follow Markovian patterns, and failure rates at each stage are constant, with the number of stages increasing exponentially. The system's performance is analyzed using a doubly exponential series expansion, which is then linked to the well-known PH-renewal process to derive a series solution up to the first doubly exponential term. The load formula is obtained through the solution of a nonlinear matrix equation, which is confirmed by comparison with known results for M/M/c and A2/M/1 queueing systems. The proposed method is demonstrated using a case study and further enhanced to accommodate multiple identical servers. The study concludes with future directions and potential applications of the findings.

A novel approach using graph neural networks, particularly distance-weighted graphs, has emerged as a viable solution for this complex problem. This study introduces a method for generating standardized and reproducible models that can be used to automate the assessment of coronary artery calcification. Overall, the results suggest that a wide range of feature extraction methods can be used to automate coronary calcium assessment with high reproducibility. Data discretization is a crucial step in the process of machine learning, as it enhances the performance of various machine learning models. In this study, we introduce a new standard for discretization that prioritizes relevance and minimizes divergence. Our proposed method, called Max-Relevance-Min-Divergence discretization, incorporates a novel information-based score to evaluate the relevance of each bin and a modified Kullback-Leibler score to quantify divergence. By maximizing relevance while minimizing divergence, MRM-D consistently outperforms other discretization methods on multiple UCI datasets, particularly when used with naive Bayes. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that MRM-D's effectiveness is not limited to naive Bayes and can be successfully applied to other machine learning models. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset, ForestFire, to showcase the potential of MRM-D in real-world machine learning tasks. Our findings confirm that MRM-D's performance is superior to other discretization methods in both simulated and real-world settings. In this research, we aim to improve the accuracy of gender identification in overlapping conversational dialogue by leveraging pre-trained audio models. We utilize the WavLM pre-training method, which is based on a large language model and utilizes a diverse range of audio data, including news articles and radio shows. This research introduces the concept of Temporal Change Reinforcement Learning (TCRL), where an agent navigates through an environment that evolves over time, requiring it to adapt to shifting rewards and transition rules. Driven by its long-term objectives, the agent must learn to operate within this dynamic setting. Diverging from traditional Reinforcement Learning, TCRL's dynamic nature necessitates the development of a novel approach to strike a balance between short-term and long-term decision-making. Our proposed solution is Temporal Change Actor-Critic (TCA3), an algorithm capable of capturing temporal changes in rewards and transitions, and has been demonstrated to be effective through comprehensive testing on various temporal change scenarios, including tasks with rewards that change over time, or vice versa. Experimental results confirm that TCA3 can successfully adapt to and perform well in these dynamic environments. Our work also provides a framework for agents to adapt to changing conditions, and our proposed algorithm can serve as a foundation for future studies on RL in dynamic environments. as a blockchain transaction processor, enforcing a set of security properties defined using

studies, including authentication protocols and a voting system. The case studies reveal the
challenges of synthesizing intelligent contracts for complex security properties, highlighting

Go's lightweight concurrency model has made it a popular choice for large projects, yet its growing complexity poses the risk of hidden concurrency issues. Theoretically, Go's lightweight gorilla and absence of Java-style locks are designed to minimize concurrency bugs, but this could be misleading. This research presents BinGo, a tool that analyzes Go binary code to identify potential concurrency flaws. The analysis is based on a Go program's execution, not its source code, which allows for the detection of concurrency-related bugs such as deadlocks, data races, and more. The tool's capabilities are demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation using 100 Go programs, of which 17 are flawed and 7 are racey. The results show that BinGo can accurately identify 14 of the 17 issues and partially detect 3 complex ones, while also detecting 4 out of the 7 racey programs. The analysis also highlights the limitations of BinGo, which are mainly due to the lack of information in the binary code. In the ALICE experiment, a custom-made detector, known as the Inner Tracking Global Tracking detector, is utilized for measuring the production of the ${\mathrm J}/\psi$ meson in collisions at the LHC. This paper details the construction and functioning of this detector, which is situated near the interaction point. It is a cylindrical device consisting of six silicon telescope layers that enables precise tracking of charged particles. Each layer is composed of a silicon pad detector and a double-sided strip detector, with the latter featuring advanced readout chips. These detectors are designed to maintain high efficiency even at the closest distance from the interaction point. Notably, a novel method of reading out the outermost layer was employed, which involves using a laser to transfer data to a dedicated photodiode. Additionally, a device called the Chip-on-Tip technology was introduced, which involves attaching a readout chip to the sensor. This innovative approach allows for real-time data collection and minimizes interference with the device's sensitive areas. The detector's silicon sensors are fabricated using 150 nm CMOS technology, which is notable for its high radiation resistance. These sensors are also designed to be resistant to high levels of neutron irradiation, with the ability to withstand 1 MRad of total ionizing dose. This paper will discuss the performance of the detector during the LHC's Run 2, with a focus on its ability to measure the production of the ${\mathrm J}/\psi$ meson. It will also present the results of the detector's performance, with a view to its future use in the LHC's Run 3. A software call graph is a crucial tool for optimizing software performance and analyzing its behavior. However, creating such a graph for a large and complex program with many lines of code can be extremely time-consuming and impractical. Our approach involves using a repository of source code to identify patterns in how different versions of a program are executed, and to create a more accurate call graph for a given system by identifying the most relevant lines of code. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we have applied it to a real-world system and shown that it can produce high-quality call graphs with a remarkably small amount of code, while also preserving the overall structure of the program. The resulting call graph is then used to identify areas of the program that are most in need of optimization. Our research highlights the potential benefits of using evolving software systems to create call graphs for a given program, and we believe that this approach has the potential to greatly accelerate the process of creating these complex graphs. Hyperspectral images are highly valuable for various applications but their utility is severely compromised by noise inherent in the acquisition process. Noise in hyperspectral images follows a specific spatial pattern and spectral profile, which makes it challenging to remove through traditional restoration techniques. In response, a novel framework is proposed to restore HSI data. The framework is composed of two key components: a spatial-spectral cross focus network and a spatial-spectral attention module. The former is designed to learn spatial-spectral relationships within HSI data, while the latter helps the network focus on relevant spatial-spectral information. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method on several benchmark datasets, which outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy. A groundbreaking approach to modeling complex astrophysical phenomena has been achieved by introducing adjoint methods into the high-dimensional models. This innovative technique enables the calculation of optimal initial conditions that minimize discrepancies between simulated and actual observations. By reformulating the problem as an optimization task, it becomes possible to utilize gradient-based optimization methods, thereby significantly improving computational efficiency. Furthermore, the use of adjoint methods allows for the calculation of uncertainties in the optimal initial conditions, providing a more robust estimate of the overall confidence level. By applying this technique to a specific problem, namely identifying the initial conditions of a supernova explosion from its light curve, we demonstrate its potential to enhance understanding of complex astrophysical phenomena, particularly in cases where direct measurement of key variables is challenging or impractical. Moreover, we show that our method can be seamlessly integrated into a high-fidelity simulation code, enabling the development of a more efficient and reliable tool for analyzing and predicting complex astrophysical events. By doing so, we aim to accelerate the discovery of complex astrophysical phenomena, ultimately contributing to the development of a more accurate and efficient method for modeling and predicting such events. A new approach to calculating the bandwidth of exciton-polariton condensates has been developed using the Bogoliubov theory of exciton-polariton lasers, which takes into account the non-trivial momentum distribution of excitons. This approach results in an explicit equation for the excitation spectrum of exciton-polariton condensates, which can be applied to various systems of exciton-polaritons confined in a quadratic potential. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have been widely adopted for solving a wide range of complex coupled ordinary differential equations (ODERs). However, the lack of universally accepted metrics for evaluating the performance of PINNs has hindered their development. To address this, we introduce a new set of metrics tailored for assessing the accuracy of PINNs in ODERs, focusing on both the global and local aspects of the solution. To ensure that these metrics are effective, we propose a simple and efficient approach for constructing neural networks with varying levels of complexity. By using these metrics, we can quantify the trade-off between the computational efficiency of PINNs and their ability to accurately represent the underlying physical phenomena. Our approach is demonstrated using multiple challenging ODERs, revealing that even simple PINNs can achieve impressive accuracy with minimal overfitting, with some models requiring only a few hundred parameters to accurately capture the complex dynamics of the underlying ODERs. Our work aims to establish a standardized framework for evaluating the performance of PINNs in solving ODERs, facilitating further research in this area. Our code is available for public use. In video conferencing, high-quality video transmission is essential, but it is hindered by the significant bandwidth requirements of high-resolution video, and the degradation that occurs due to encoding and decoding processes. To address this issue, our proposed system, Gemino, utilizes neural compression to reduce video bandwidth needs and implements a novel, lightweight, and robust loss-tolerant framework that minimizes errors during decoding and transmission. By leveraging the capabilities of edge devices to compress video, Gemino enables efficient transmission even under poor network conditions, and our experimental results demonstrate that it achieves a substantial reduction in bandwidth usage, up to 20x, while maintaining video quality comparable to the original, and outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.
